definition.text: A message queue is a software component, typically used for communication between processes or threads, that holds messages in a queue until the receiver takes them.

facts.text: Message queues implement asynchronous communication: the sending and receiving parties do not need to interact with the queue at the same time.
Messages placed onto the queue are stored until the recipient retrieves them.
The message queue paradigm is a sibling of the publisher/subscriber pattern and is typically one part of a larger message-oriented middleware system.

An administrator configures queue-manager or broker software and defines a named queue; an application registers a routine that listens for messages, and other applications connect and put messages onto the queue.
The queue manager stores the messages until a receiving application connects, then calls the registered routine, and the application processes the message.
Queues have implicit or explicit limits on the size of a single message and on the number of messages that may remain outstanding.
Queuing systems that connect different computer systems typically provide resilience functionality so that messages do not get lost when a system fails.
Queue software can be proprietary, open source or a mix, and runs either on private servers or as an external cloud message queuing service.

definition.text: In synchronous communication the sender waits for a reply, as with an HTTP request; in asynchronous communication the sender carries on without waiting.

facts.text: Many widely known communications protocols operate synchronously; HTTP is the obvious example, where a user requests a web page and then waits for the reply.
Synchronous behaviour is not always appropriate: an application may need to notify another that an event occurred without waiting for a response.
In publish/subscribe an application publishes information for any number of clients to read, and the sender should not have to wait if a recipient has crashed.
Applications need not be exclusively one or the other: an interactive application can answer part of a request at once and queue other parts, such as billing, to be done later.
A subsystem that performs message queuing, or broadcast messaging, can improve the behaviour of the overall system in these situations.
Asynchronous behaviour can be layered over a synchronous request-response protocol, which is how some queue services work over HTTP, though the underlying protocol limits what they can offer.

definition.text: Queueing systems let you choose between several semantics, such as durability, time to live, filtering and delivery guarantees, that affect reliability and efficiency.

facts.text: Durability: messages may be kept in memory, written to disk, or even committed to a database when reliability calls for a more resource-intensive solution.
Queues or messages may have a time to live, and some systems filter data so a subscriber sees only messages matching pre-specified criteria.
Delivery policies decide whether a message must be delivered at least once or no more than once; routing policies decide which servers receive a message in a system with many queue servers.
Batching policies, the criteria for when a message counts as enqueued, and receipt notification for publishers all have substantial effects on transaction semantics, reliability and efficiency.

definition.text: Message queuing historically used closed proprietary protocols; open standards such as AMQP, STOMP and MQTT now exist for open source implementations.

facts.text: Message queuing has historically used proprietary, closed protocols, and Sun's JMS specification gave only a Java-only abstraction of a client API.

Three standards are used in open source queues: AMQP, a feature-rich protocol approved as ISO/IEC 19464 since April 2014; STOMP, a simple text-oriented protocol; and MQTT, a lightweight protocol especially for embedded devices.
AMQP and STOMP operate at the same level as HTTP, while MQTT operates at the level of TCP/IP.
Some proprietary implementations, such as Amazon's SQS, use HTTP because asynchronous behaviour can always be layered over request-response semantics, but they are constrained by that protocol.

definition.text: Delivery semantics describe how many times a message reaches its consumer: at most once, at least once, or exactly once.

facts.text: At-most-once delivery means a message is delivered not more than once: messages may be lost but are not redelivered.
At-most-once suits use cases such as monitoring metrics, where a small amount of data loss is acceptable.
At-least-once delivery loses no message but may deliver the same message several times.
At-least-once is usually good enough when duplication is not a big issue or the consumer can deduplicate, for example by rejecting a duplicate write on a message's unique key.
Most message brokers offer at-least-once delivery, so consumers will eventually see duplicates.
Exactly-once is the most difficult semantic to implement; it is friendly to users but costs a lot in performance and complexity.
Exactly-once matters for financial use cases such as payment, trading and accounting, especially when duplication is unacceptable and the downstream service does not support idempotency.

definition.text: A message broker is an intermediary program that translates messages between the messaging protocols of sender and receiver and validates, stores, routes and delivers them.

facts.text: A broker translates a message from the sender's formal messaging protocol to the receiver's, so services written in different languages or on different platforms can talk to each other.
Brokers act as intermediaries, so senders issue messages without knowing where the receivers are, whether they are active, or how many there are, which decouples processes and services.
A broker may manage a workload queue or message queue for multiple receivers, providing reliable storage, guaranteed message delivery and perhaps transaction management.
Brokers can route messages to one or more destinations, transform messages to another representation, and provide content and topic-based routing using the publish–subscribe pattern.
Brokers offer two basic message distribution patterns: point-to-point messaging, as in message queues, and publish-subscribe messaging, where producers publish to topics that consumers subscribe to.
Message brokers are generally based on one of two architectures: hub-and-spoke, where a central server provides integration services, or a message bus acting as a communication backbone.

title: Message broker versus event streaming platform

definition.text: Message brokers support several messaging patterns with delivery tracking, while event streaming platforms offer pub/sub distribution of stored topic streams at higher scale.

facts.text: Message brokers can support two or more messaging patterns, including message queues and pub/sub, while event streaming platforms only offer pub/sub-style distribution.
Event streaming platforms are designed for high volumes of messages, are readily scalable, and order streams of records into topics stored for a predetermined amount of time.
Unlike message brokers, event streaming platforms cannot guarantee message delivery or track which consumers have received the messages.
Event streaming platforms offer more scalability than brokers but fewer fault-tolerance features such as message resending, and more limited routing and queueing capabilities.

notes: Singh's generalisation about event streaming platforms; the Kafka guides in the event-streaming chapter describe configurable delivery guarantees, so check that the writer states this as Singh's comparison.

definition.text: An enterprise service bus is an architectural pattern in which a centralized software component performs integrations between applications.

facts.text: An ESB performs data-model transformations, handles connectivity, routes messages, converts communication protocols and may manage the composition of multiple requests, exposing these integrations as reusable service interfaces.
In theory a centralized ESB can standardize and simplify communication and integration across the enterprise, letting components scale independently and fail without affecting others.
In many organizations the ESB came to be seen as a bottleneck: a single point of failure can bring down all communications, and a change to one integration can destabilize others.
Message brokers are a lightweight alternative to ESBs that offer inter-service communication at lower cost and suit microservices architectures, as ESBs have fallen out of favor.

definition.text: Cloud messaging patterns are named designs for how services exchange messages, such as asynchronous request-reply, claim check, saga and competing consumers.

facts.text: Asynchronous request-reply decouples backend processing from clients for long-running tasks, with the API answering HTTP 202 (Accepted) to acknowledge the request.
Publisher-subscriber decouples senders from consumers and avoids blocking the sender to wait for a response.
Claim check handles large messages by storing the whole payload in a database and transmitting only a reference, which is later used to retrieve the payload.
Priority queue lets requests with a higher priority be received and processed more quickly than those with a lower priority.
Saga manages data consistency across services that each own a database, without distributed transactions, which are difficult to scale and can hurt performance.
Competing consumers lets multiple concurrent consumers process messages from the same channel without complex coordination, but cannot guarantee message ordering.

definition.text: The competing consumers pattern lets several consumers process messages from the same queue at the same time.

facts.text: The Competing Consumers pattern enables multiple concurrent consumers to process messages on the same message queue.
There is no need to configure complex coordination between the consumers.
The pattern cannot guarantee message ordering.

definition.text: A queue is a widely used data structure that takes new elements at one end and gives them back from the other; common variants are FIFO, circular, priority and double-ended queues.

facts.text: A simple queue follows FIFO: a new element is inserted at the tail and an element is removed from the head, so emails for payment responses go out in the same order.
A circular queue, also called a circular buffer or ring buffer, links its last element to its first; LMAX's low-latency ring buffer, used by trading components, runs in memory.
Elements of a priority queue have predefined priorities, and the one with the highest or lowest priority is taken first; it is implemented with a max heap or min heap.
A deque, or double-ended queue, allows insertion and deletion at both head and tail, so it supports both FIFO and LIFO and can implement a stack.

definition.text: A blocking queue algorithm uses locks so a waiting thread is suspended, while a non-blocking algorithm rejects access immediately instead of making the thread wait.

facts.text: A blocking algorithm uses locks: if Thread A is suspended while holding the lock, Thread B may wait for arbitrarily long periods and can starve.
A non-blocking algorithm notifies Thread B that access is rejected rather than blocking it until the lock is released, though other threads may still starve due to rejections.
Wait-free means all threads complete their tasks within a finite number of steps, which is non-blocking plus starvation-free.
A non-blocking queue can be implemented with compare and swap (CAS), and with no thread suspension and no lock waiting, latency drops and deadlock cannot occur.

definition.text: Operating systems and applications provide message queues that exist only for that system, such as the UNIX SYS V and POSIX queues and the event queues of graphical interfaces.

facts.text: Many message queue implementations function internally within an operating system or an application, and such queues exist for the purposes of that system only.
UNIX has two common message queue implementations, one in the SYS V API and a later, distinct but similar one in POSIX.
In SYS V a blocking receive puts the caller to sleep until a message of the requested type is posted, while a non-blocking receive returns immediately to report that it failed.
Graphical user interfaces use a message queue, also called an event queue, to pass mouse, keyboard and timer events to the application, which removes them one at a time in an event loop.

definition.text: Choose a message queue by comparing speed, scalability, reliability, durability, ease of use, ecosystem, integration and protocol support.

facts.text: Compare speed, scalability, reliability (messages are not lost), durability (messages kept safe over time), ease of setup and management, ecosystem tools, integration with other software, and the protocols and languages supported.

Decide the pattern first: queues give one-to-one point-to-point delivery and pub/sub lets many consumers subscribe to a topic; brokers can offer both, while event streaming platforms offer only pub/sub.

Event streaming platforms scale more and are built for high volumes, but cannot guarantee delivery or track which consumers received messages, and offer fewer fault-tolerance features and less routing.

Match the delivery guarantee to the need: most brokers offer at-least-once, so consumers see duplicates, and exactly-once costs performance and complexity; MQTT orders its levels by increasing overhead.
Check the ordering guarantee: most queues give best-effort ordering, SQS FIFO orders only within a message group, and MQTT only within one client session on one topic.

Protocol matters for interoperability: JMS is an API, so JMS systems from different vendors are not interoperable, while AMQP is wire-level so compliant software interoperates; MQTT targets constrained devices.
Look for failure handling and limits: a dead-letter queue sets unprocessable messages aside, and SQS caps message bodies at 256KB, with larger payloads stored elsewhere and referenced by pointer.
Check availability beyond one node: MQTT leaves broker-to-broker communication to implementations, and ActiveMQ offers locking-based failover, ZooKeeper replication and a Network of Brokers.

definition.text: Publish–subscribe is a messaging pattern in which publishers send messages to topics without knowing the receivers, and subscribers receive only the topics they asked for.

facts.text: Publishers categorize messages into classes, or topics, and send them without needing to know which components will receive them.
Subscribers express interest in one or more classes and receive only messages in those classes, without needing to know who the publishers are.
The pattern decouples the components that produce messages from those that consume them and supports asynchronous, many-to-many communication.
A message published to a topic is pushed immediately to all subscribers, which often perform different functions and can each act on the message in parallel.
Pub/sub is contrasted with queue-based and point-to-point messaging, where producers send directly to consumers; JMS, Apache Kafka and MQTT support both the pub/sub and queue-based models.
It gives greater network scalability and more dynamic topologies, but can make it harder to modify the publisher's logic or the structure of the published data.
Compared with synchronous patterns such as RPC, pub/sub gives the highest decoupling, but it can lead to semantic or format coupling that makes systems entangled or brittle over time.
Pub/sub is now distinguished from the observer pattern by its emphasis on decoupling, asynchronous messaging and broker-mediated communication across a distributed system.

title: Message queue versus publish–subscribe

definition.text: A message queue gives each message to one consumer, while publish–subscribe delivers each message to every subscriber of a topic.

facts.text: In a message queue each message is processed only once by a single consumer, while in pub/sub all subscribers to the topic receive every message broadcast.
Queues hold messages until they are retrieved, whereas topics transfer messages with little or no queuing and push them out immediately to all subscribers.
With a message queue the sender often knows the destination it sends to, while in pub/sub the publisher need not know who uses its information and subscribers need not know where it comes from.
Most messaging systems support both models in their API, for example the Java Message Service.

notes: no section of its own: the contrast is drawn on the Wikipedia and Singh pub/sub pages and the Singh message-queue page

definition.text: Filtering is how a pub/sub system selects the messages a subscriber receives, by topic, by content, or by both.

facts.text: In pub/sub systems subscribers typically receive only a subset of messages, and the process of selecting the relevant ones is called filtering.
Topic-based filtering publishes messages to named topics or channels, and subscribers who register for a topic receive all messages published to it.
Content-based filtering lets subscribers define constraints on message attributes or content, and messages are delivered only if they match.
Hybrid systems categorize messages by topic and let subscribers apply content-based filters to the messages within those topics.

definition.text: Pub/sub systems connect publishers and subscribers either through a central broker or event bus, or directly in a brokerless arrangement.

facts.text: In most pub/sub systems publishers and subscribers communicate through a central intermediary such as a message broker or event bus.

Subscriber registration can happen at build time, with handlers hardcoded as in GUI event handlers; at initialization time, with subscriptions in XML configuration or metadata; or at runtime, added and removed dynamically.

Brokerless pub/sub systems let publishers and subscribers discover each other and exchange messages directly; the Data Distribution Service middleware uses IP multicast and metadata sharing to set up communication paths.

definition.text: Publish–subscribe lets publishers and subscribers work independently, avoids polling, and makes it easy to add or remove subscribers.

facts.text: Publishers are loosely coupled to subscribers and need not know they exist; with the topic as the focus, each side stays ignorant of system topology and operates independently of the other.
Many pub/sub systems also decouple publishers and subscribers in time, unlike the client-server paradigm, where neither side can post or receive while the other is not running.
Push-based delivery through topics removes the need for consumers to poll for updates, which gives faster response time and lower delivery latency.
A publisher simply posts to a topic instead of keeping a roster of peers, and subscribers can change, upgrade, multiply or disappear while the system adjusts dynamically.

Publishers and subscribers can be developed and scaled independently, and pub/sub can scale better than client-server through parallel operation, message caching and tree-based or network-based routing.
Redundant subscribers can assure delivery with minimal added complexity: an exact duplicate of a logging subscriber can be added without any impact on other equipment.

Internet-wide RSS and Atom syndication shows pub/sub scaling beyond a single data center, accepting higher latency and no delivery guarantees so a low-end web server can reach millions of subscribers.

definition.text: The main drawbacks of publish–subscribe come from decoupling: delivery is hard to guarantee, and large systems can become unstable.

facts.text: The most serious problems are a side-effect of decoupling, and a broker that stops delivering after a specified time cannot guarantee delivery, so assured delivery needs tighter coupling such as receipt messages from subscribers.
A publisher may assume a subscriber is listening when it is not, and will not necessarily be told if a subscriber such as a logger fails.
Pub/sub scales well for small networks with low message volume, but as nodes and messages grow, instabilities such as load surges and slowdowns limit the maximum scalability.
Brokers can be overloaded tracking subscriptions or fooled into notifying the wrong client, and encryption cannot stop authorized publishers from introducing damaging messages.

definition.text: Pub/sub services typically add fanout to many kinds of endpoints, durable storage of messages, and authentication of publishers.

facts.text: Topics can typically connect to multiple types of endpoints, such as message queues, serverless functions and HTTP servers.
Fanout happens when a message sent to a topic is replicated and pushed to multiple endpoints, giving asynchronous event notifications that allow parallel processing.
Pub/sub services often provide very high durability and at-least-once delivery by storing copies of the same message on multiple servers.
Topics authenticate applications that try to publish, which allows encrypted endpoints and encryption of messages in transit over the network.

definition.text: Message queues let a system scale, decouple its components, respond faster and survive failures by putting a buffer between producers and consumers.

facts.text: Queues are used to manage requests in large-scale distributed systems, where writes that are predictably fast in small systems can take an almost non-deterministic amount of time.
Scalability: queues make it possible to scale where needed, and at peak load multiple instances of an application can add requests to the queue without risk of collision.
Decoupling: queues remove dependencies between components and simplify the implementation of decoupled applications.
Performance: endpoints that produce and consume messages interact with the queue, not each other, so producers can add requests without waiting for them to be processed.
Reliability: queues make data persistent and reduce the errors that happen when different parts of the system go offline.

title: How a message queue processes jobs

definition.text: A producer puts a job on the queue and a consumer later takes it off, processes it and reports completion.

facts.text: A producer publishes a job to the queue and then notifies the user of the job status.
A consumer picks up the job from the queue, processes it, then signals that the job is complete.
Messages are stored in the queue until they are processed and deleted.
Each message is processed only once by a single consumer.

definition.text: Message queues commonly offer delayed delivery, delivery guarantees, dead-letter queues, ordering, poison pills, authentication and task queues.

facts.text: Many queues support setting a specific delivery time for a message, and a delay queue gives all messages a common delay.
Queues may store multiple copies for redundancy and resend messages after failures to deliver at least once, while FIFO queues filter out duplicates automatically to deliver exactly once.
A dead-letter queue receives messages other queues cannot process successfully, so they can be inspected later without blocking processing or wasting CPU on a message that may never succeed.
Most queues give best-effort ordering, so messages are generally delivered in the order sent and at least once; in a FIFO queue the oldest entry, the head, is processed first.
Poison pills are special messages that can be received but not processed; they signal a consumer to end its work, much like closing a socket in a client/server model.
Queues authenticate applications that try to access them, which allows messages to be encrypted over the network and in the queue itself.
Task queues receive tasks and their data, run them and deliver the results, can support scheduling, and can run computationally intensive jobs in the background.

definition.text: Consumers either pull messages by repeatedly asking the queue for new ones, or have the queue push each message to them when it arrives.

facts.text: Most message queues provide both push and pull options for retrieving messages.
Pull means continuously querying the queue for new messages, and push means a consumer is notified when a message is available.
Long-polling allows pulls to wait a specified amount of time for new messages to arrive.
Pub/sub topics push notifications instantly, which eliminates the need for consumers to poll for new information.

definition.text: Backpressure limits the size of a queue so that a growing backlog does not slow down the jobs already in it.

facts.text: If a queue grows beyond memory, the result is cache misses, disk reads and even slower performance.
Backpressure limits the queue size, which maintains a high throughput rate and good response times for jobs already in the queue.
Once the queue fills up, clients get a server-busy or HTTP 503 status code to try again later.
Clients can retry the request at a later time, perhaps with an exponential backoff strategy.

definition.text: RabbitMQ is an open-source message broker, written in Erlang, that originally implemented AMQP and supports other protocols through plug-ins.

facts.text: RabbitMQ originally implemented the Advanced Message Queuing Protocol and has been extended through a plug-in architecture to support STOMP, MQTT and other protocols.
Written in Erlang, the server is built on the Open Telecom Platform framework for clustering and failover.
Client libraries for the broker are available for all major programming languages.

Plug-ins include Shovel, which moves or copies messages from one broker to another; Federation, which shares messages between brokers at the exchange level; and Management, which monitors and controls brokers and clusters.
RabbitMQ uses Raft to implement durable, replicated FIFO queues.
System designs place jobs on a queue such as Amazon SQS or RabbitMQ, for example for notifications, video processing and extracting transactions from accounts.

definition.text: A dead letter queue is a place where a messaging system stores messages that it cannot or should not deliver.

facts.text: Depending on the implementation, a message goes to the dead letter queue if its queue does not exist, its time to live expires, another queue exchange rejects it, or it was read and rejected too many times.
Setting such messages aside lets the main queue keep moving: they can be inspected later without blocking processing or spending CPU cycles on a message that may never be consumed successfully.
Routing failed messages to a dead letter queue enables analysis of common fault patterns and potential software problems.
A consumer that considers a message invalid can forward it to an Invalid Message Channel, which separates application-level faults from delivery failures.
Managing dead letter queues typically involves monitoring and alerting, and organizations may add specialized handlers for automated remediation or manual processing of the messages.

In an SQS FIFO queue, later messages in a message group wait until the preceding one is processed or moved to the dead-letter queue; once there it is no longer retried, leaving a gap, and the rest continue in order.
Many systems offer dead letter queues, including Amazon SQS and EventBridge, Apache ActiveMQ, Google Cloud Pub/Sub, Azure Service Bus, RabbitMQ and Apache Pulsar.

definition.text: Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) is a distributed message queuing service from Amazon.

facts.text: SQS is a distributed message queuing service that supports both unlimited queues and unlimited message traffic; messages can be of any type.
SQS provides queuing over HTTP; asynchronous behaviour can always be layered over request-response semantics, but such an implementation is constrained by the underlying protocol.
SQS FIFO queues guarantee ordering within a message group but do not necessarily guarantee ordered delivery across retries or failures.
Message bodies are limited to 256KB; a larger message can be split into segments, or its data can be stored in Amazon S3 or DynamoDB with only a pointer sent in the SQS message.

definition.text: AMQP is an open standard application layer protocol for message-oriented middleware.

facts.text: AMQP is a wire-level protocol: it describes the format of the bytes sent across the network, so any compliant tool can interoperate with any other regardless of language, unlike API-level standards such as JMS.

Its defining features are message orientation, queuing, routing (point-to-point and publish-and-subscribe), reliability and security; it is a binary protocol that assumes a reliable transport such as TCP.
AMQP provides flow-controlled messaging with at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery guarantees, plus authentication and encryption based on SASL and TLS.
Messages travel one way over a link using transfer frames; credit-based flow control keeps a receiver from being overwhelmed and lets a subscribing link pull messages when it wants them.

Every transferred message must eventually be settled, so sender and receiver agree on the transfer's state; this settlement is how the at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once guarantees are enforced.

The bare message the application created is immutable in transit, so end-to-end signing, encryption and integrity checks stay valid; intermediaries add annotations kept separate from it, and a header carries time to live, durability and priority.

Queues and topics are distribution nodes; AMQP codifies accept and reject outcomes, competing and non-competing consumers (the move and copy distribution modes), filters, and on-demand temporary nodes.

Version 1.0 focuses on the core features needed for Internet-scale interoperability and has less explicit routing than earlier versions; broker implementations include Apache Qpid, ActiveMQ, Solace and RabbitMQ 4.0.

definition.text: MQTT is a lightweight publish-subscribe network protocol for machine-to-machine messaging.

facts.text: MQTT suits devices with limited resources or network bandwidth, such as Internet of things sensors; it runs over an ordered, lossless transport, typically TCP/IP, and despite its name provides publish-subscribe messaging with no queues.

Clients connect to a broker, which receives messages from publishers and routes them to subscribers by topic; publishers need no knowledge of subscribers, so devices and server applications stay decoupled.
A broker discards a message with no current subscribers unless it is flagged retained; it keeps one retained message per topic and delivers it to each new subscriber immediately.
A publisher can register a default message at connect time that the broker sends to subscribers if it detects an unexpected disconnect.

Each connection chooses a quality of service in increasing order of overhead: at most once (fire and forget), at least once (acknowledged, retried) or exactly once (two-level handshake); it applies between MQTT sender and receiver, not to TCP.
With persistent sessions the broker stores each client's connection info, subscriptions and any QoS 1 or 2 messages while the device goes on and off.

The specification covers only a client talking to one broker; larger deployments use bridging, where a broker connects to another as a client, or clustering, where broker nodes share subscription and session state as one logical broker.

MQTT guarantees ordering only within one client session on one topic, so messages from independent clients can arrive out of order; mitigations are debounce windows, polling and sequence numbers, each with trade-offs.

definition.text: Message-oriented middleware is software or hardware infrastructure that supports sending and receiving messages between distributed systems.

facts.text: It insulates application developers from the details of operating systems and network interfaces, so independently developed components on different platforms can interact.
RPC- and ORB-based middleware create tightly coupled components, where a caller waits for the called procedure to return; message-oriented systems allow loose coupling.
The sender calls the provider and carries on, confident the provider keeps the message until a receiver retrieves it; queues buffer for a busy or disconnected receiver, and most systems persist them.
Sender and receiver need not be online together, and if the receiver fails, senders continue unaffected as messages accumulate in the queue until it restarts.
The provider can store, route or transform messages in transit, so one application can send in its native format and several others each receive a copy in their own format.
The main disadvantage is an extra component, the message broker, which can reduce performance and reliability and make the system harder and costlier to maintain.
Asynchronous messaging fits poorly where a sender must wait for a reply, though most systems can group request and response into one pseudo-synchronous transaction.
A sender in a loosely coupled system can keep piling work on a recipient until its resources run out and it fails, so message flow must be monitored and adjusted.

definition.text: Apache ActiveMQ is an open source message broker written in Java together with a full Java Message Service client.

facts.text: ActiveMQ is an open source broker written in Java with a full JMS client; Java uses JMS 1.1 and other languages use cross-language clients.
It supports several transport protocols: OpenWire, STOMP, MQTT, AMQP, REST and WebSockets.
ActiveMQ Classic gets high availability from file-system or database row-level locking, a shared persistence store, or replication using ZooKeeper, and scales horizontally with a Network of Brokers.
Artemis, based on the HornetQ code base, is the next-generation broker under the ActiveMQ umbrella: multi-protocol, embeddable, clustered and asynchronous.

definition.text: NATS is an open-source messaging system under the stewardship of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation.

facts.text: The NATS server is written in Go, with client libraries for dozens of languages; its core design principles are performance, scalability and ease of use.

Core NATS is the publish-subscribe server; JetStream is an optional built-in persistence layer adding streaming, queues, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery, replay, flow control and a key/value store.
JetStream replaced the older STAN (NATS Streaming) approach and uses the Raft consensus algorithm for cluster management and data replication.

definition.text: In the observer pattern a subject keeps a list of observers and automatically notifies them of state changes, typically by calling one of their methods.

facts.text: It sets up a one-to-many dependency without tight coupling: observers register and unregister themselves with the subject, which only needs to know they implement an update operation.
Subject and observers hold direct references with no intermediary broker, and notification is typically synchronous, so the pattern suits in-process uses such as GUI toolkits.

Publish-subscribe adds a broker so publishers and subscribers are unaware of each other; it scales to distributed systems, filters by topic and isolates failures, whereas observer failures can affect the subject.
The pattern deliberately omits unsubscription, filtering, delivery guarantees and message logging, which robust message queuing systems provide.
